Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

could you turn this into a clear request for a comparison of pond care options? i have a small backyard pond and three possible routines from notes i got, and want them compared side by side rather than a general guide to ponds. the pond is about 9 feet by 6 feet and 22 inches at its deepest point, with a shallow shelf along one side. it holds roughly 500 gallons, though that number is an estimate from the previous owner. it has a small waterfall, a pump, and a box filter. there are six goldfish, water lilies, and some submerged plants. the pond gets sun from late morning until about 3 p.m. in summer, and a maple tree overhangs the north edge. leaves start falling into it in september. the water sometimes looks green by july, but i don't have test results or a record of how often that happens. don't treat the green water as a diagnosis.

these are the routines to compare, please stick to the details listed and don't fill in missing features. option A is the routine i've been doing: run the pump and waterfall continuously from spring through fall, rinse the filter box sponge in a bucket of pond water every two weeks during summer, and remove leaves with a net when i notice them. i top up water with a garden hose when the level drops. i have not been adding treatments or doing scheduled water changes. in winter i unplug the waterfall when freezing weather is expected, but the pump stays on in a deeper part of the pond. i don't know the pump's flow rate or how much electricity it uses.

option B is a low-equipment routine suggested by a neighbor. it uses a floating leaf net from early fall until most leaves are down, with leaf removal from the net about twice a week. the neighbor says to keep the existing pump and filter running during the warm months and to clean the sponge when flow slows, rather than on a set calendar. the routine includes topping up as needed, and trimming dead plant leaves. there is no stated schedule for winter, no water-change instruction, and no added product listed. the neighbor called it “less fuss, same pond,” but that is their description, not a measurement.

option C is a more scheduled routine from a local pond shop handout. it says to check the pump intake and filter once a week in summer, rinse filter media in removed pond water when dirty, and clear leaves from the pond daily during heavy fall leaf drop. it also lists a partial water change of about 10 percent once a month from May through September, and says to use a dechlorinator when adding tap water. the handout recommends testing water monthly for pH, ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate, but does not give target readings in the excerpt i have. for winter it says to stop the waterfall before ice forms and keep a small opening in the ice with an air stone. it doesn't state the air stone size, exact placement, product brand, or cost.

please compare the three routines only on the criteria below, using the information above. if a detail isn't supplied, flag it as not specified instead of guessing. don't assume the options are proven to work equally well, and don't say that any routine is safe for these fish without evidence.

1. routine and time commitment: explain the stated frequency of checking, cleaning, leaf removal, topping up, water changes, and winter steps. separate scheduled tasks from tasks triggered by conditions such as slow flow or visible leaves.
2. equipment and supplies: identify what each option says to use, including equipment already present, the leaf net, test kit, dechlorinator, and air stone. distinguish existing equipment from additional items; where a size, brand, or cost is missing, say so.
3. monitoring and water-management details: compare which options include testing, what is tested, and whether they give targets. include the stated water-change amounts and timing, and explain that the pond volume is an estimate. don't infer water quality from appearance alone.
4. seasonal coverage and practical tradeoffs: compare what each routine says for warm months, fall leaves, and winter, and note any seasonal directions that are absent. mention the overhanging maple, lilies and submerged plants, fish, sun exposure, and existing pump/filter setup only where relevant to understanding the scope; don't add care advice for them.

use a compact table if useful, followed by a short neutral summary of the main differences. keep the wording practical for a pond owner, preserve that the neighbor's phrase is a quote, and don't choose a preferred option, add a fourth routine, estimate costs or labor, or supply general pond-care instructions. one more thing, the source notes don't say whether the fish stay in the pond over winter or how cold it gets here, so leave those points open rather than making assumptions.", "output": "Please compare the three pond-care routines below side by side. Keep the comparison limited to the supplied details; do not turn it into a general pond-care guide or add recommendations. Do not choose a preferred routine or assume that the options are proven to work equally well. Do not claim that any routine is safe for the fish without evidence.

## Pond details

The backyard pond is about 9 feet by 6 feet and 22 inches deep at its deepest point, with a shallow shelf along one side. Its volume is estimated at roughly 500 gallons, based on information from the previous owner. It has a small waterfall, a pump, and a box filter. There are six goldfish, water lilies, and submerged plants. In summer, the pond receives sun from late morning until about 3 p.m. A maple tree overhangs the north edge, and leaves begin falling into the pond in September. The water sometimes looks green by July, but there are no test results or record of how often this happens. Do not treat the green appearance as a diagnosis.

## Routines to compare

**Option A — Current routine:** Run the pump and waterfall continuously from spring through fall. During summer, rinse the filter-box sponge in a bucket of pond water every two weeks and remove leaves with a net when noticed. Top up with a garden hose when the water level drops. No treatments or scheduled water changes are currently used. In winter, unplug the waterfall when freezing weather is expected, while keeping the pump in a deeper part of the pond. The pump’s flow rate and electricity use are unknown.

**Option B — Neighbor’s routine:** Use a floating leaf net from early fall until most leaves have fallen, removing leaves from the net about twice a week. Keep the existing pump and filter running during warm months, and clean the sponge when flow slows rather than on a set schedule. Top up as needed and trim dead plant leaves. No winter schedule, water-change instructions, or added products are listed. The neighbor described it as “less fuss, same pond”; treat that as the neighbor’s description, not a measured result.

**Option C — Pond-shop handout:** Check the pump intake and filter weekly in summer. Rinse filter media in removed pond water when dirty, and clear leaves from the pond daily during heavy fall leaf drop. Change about 10 percent of the water once a month from May through September, using a dechlorinator when adding tap water. Test monthly for pH, ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate. The available excerpt gives no target readings. For winter, stop the waterfall before ice forms and keep a small opening in the ice with an air stone. The air stone’s size, exact placement, product brand, and cost are not stated.

## Comparison criteria

1. **Routine and time commitment:** Describe the stated frequency of checking, cleaning, leaf removal, topping up, water changes, and winter steps. Distinguish scheduled tasks from tasks triggered by conditions, such as slow flow or visible leaves.
2. **Equipment and supplies:** Identify what each routine says to use, including existing equipment, the leaf net, test kit, dechlorinator, and air stone. Distinguish existing equipment from additional items. Mark unspecified sizes, brands, or costs as not specified.
3. **Monitoring and water management:** Compare which routines include testing, which parameters are tested, and whether targets are provided. Include the stated water-change amount and timing. Note that the pond volume is an estimate, and do not infer water quality from appearance alone.
4. **Seasonal coverage and practical tradeoffs:** Compare the stated warm-month, fall-leaf, and winter steps, and note where seasonal directions are absent. Mention the maple, lilies and submerged plants, fish, sun exposure, and existing pump/filter setup only where relevant to the comparison’s scope. Do not add care advice for them.

A compact table may be followed by a short, neutral summary of the main differences. Do not add a fourth routine, estimate costs or labor, or provide general pond-care instructions. Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you help me put together a practical care plan for my backyard pond, not a redesign. it's an in-ground lined pond behind the garage, about 8 feet by 5 feet at the widest points and maybe 20 to 26 inches deep. i have always called it about 450 gallons but that's a guess, i never measured it when it was filled. the liner is intact as far as i can see and there isn't a bottom drain. please don't build the plan around draining it or taking the whole thing apart.

it's partly shaded by a maple for most of the day, with sun reaching one end in the afternoon. there are two goldfish, both roughly 4 to 5 inches and we've had them about three years. no new fish have been added. there is one water lily and three plants in baskets along the edge, but they are only just starting to grow this spring. the fish are coming up for food and swimming normally. i feed a small pinch of floating pellets once a day; sometimes i skip a day if we're away. i don't know whether that is the right amount, so include feeding guidance but don't assume i want more fish or more plants.

water has turned green over the last couple of weeks, and there's stringy algae on several of the stones. i can still see the fish when i stand by the edge, though not clearly from the patio. there are some soft leaves and brown material sitting in the shallow end. maple leaves fall in during autumn; last year's mesh net sagged into the water after rain and was awkward to lift, so i'd like a more workable way to manage leaves if there's one within the limits below. there's no bad smell and i haven't seen fish gasping, lying over, or acting differently. i don't want the plan to treat an emergency as already happening.

yesterday morning the water was 61 degrees F. a test strip read pH 7.5, nitrite 0, and nitrate about 20 ppm. i don't own an ammonia kit, and i don't know how accurate the strip is. i haven't tested alkalinity or hardness. the pond level sometimes drops an inch or two in a week, but i can't tell how much is evaporation, splashing, or a small leak; i haven't found a wet patch around the liner. when i top it up i use the garden tap. a neighbor said, "just leave the hose water sitting overnight," but i don't know whether that's suitable for our municipal water or for the fish. please address that uncertainty rather than treating the neighbor's suggestion as a fact.

there's a submersible pump with a sponge filter, installed two summers ago. the label says 500 gallons per hour, although i don't know the actual flow after the hose and filter. it runs all day and night. the outlet is on a GFCI. the pump has not stopped, but every few weeks the sponge looks brown and the flow seems weaker; i rinse it in a bucket of pond water and put it back. the return hose is about 12 feet long and sends water back over a flat rock. i have not replaced the pump, hose, or filter media. please include sensible checks and cleaning intervals for this equipment without assuming it is broken or telling me to buy a larger pump by default.

my limits are pretty modest. i can spend up to $180 before tax on useful supplies, but i'd rather use what i own when that's reasonable. i have a garden hose, two clean buckets, a hand net, a stiff brush, and gloves. i can spend two or three hours on a weekend to get things under control, then around 15 minutes a week on regular care. i can't supervise a long job during weekdays. i don't want to use algaecide, herbicide, or other pond chemicals as a first choice, and i don't want to harm the fish, plants, or visiting birds. there are two cats that sometimes watch the fish from the edge, so mention any practical safety concern about leaving tools or materials where they can reach them. don't assume the cats drink from the pond.

1) i'd like the plan to say what to do first, what can wait, and what to watch over the next few weeks, with a realistic order for one weekend rather than a giant all-at-once cleanup. include how to remove the loose leaves and algae without scrubbing everything bare or stirring all the bottom material into the water. explain what to do with the dirty water or debris, and whether partial water changes make sense here; if so, give a cautious way to approach them given that the volume is uncertain.

also explain what measurements or tests matter most next, how often to check them at first, and what readings or fish signs should change the plan. i'd like a simple recurring routine for the rest of spring and summer, plus what to adjust as leaves begin falling in autumn. our location and winter temperatures haven't been included, so tell me if local climate information is needed before making specific cold-weather recommendations rather than assuming a freeze date.

please keep the advice practical for this particular small pond, distinguish the known facts from the uncertain estimates, and give options that stay within the budget and time limits. if a recommendation depends on the actual pond volume, water chemistry, or pump flow, say what i should measure before acting. i'm looking for a usable plan, not a diagnosis that the pond has a particular disease or a promise that the water will clear by a certain day. mention when a pond professional or veterinarian would be worth contacting, but don't make the current normal fish behavior sound like an emergency. organize the answer so i can follow the immediate steps, routine care, and points to reassess without having to guess what comes next.", "output": "Create a practical care plan for my existing backyard pond, focusing on maintenance rather than redesign. Keep the recommendations appropriate to the pond and the limits below, and distinguish confirmed details from estimates or unknowns.

**Pond and fish**
- The in-ground, lined pond is behind the garage, about 8 feet by 5 feet at its widest points and 20–26 inches deep. I estimate its volume at about 450 gallons, but have never measured it when full. The liner appears intact, and there is no bottom drain.
- It is shaded by a maple for most of the day, with afternoon sun reaching one end. It has two goldfish, about 4–5 inches long, kept for roughly three years; no fish have been added. They are swimming and feeding normally.
- There is one water lily and three edge plants in baskets, just beginning to grow this spring. I feed a small pinch of floating pellets once daily and sometimes skip a day when away. Include feeding guidance, but do not assume I want more fish or plants.

**Current conditions and equipment**
The water has been green for a couple of weeks, with stringy algae on several stones. The fish are visible from the edge, though not clearly from the patio. Soft leaves and brown material have collected in the shallow end. Maple leaves fall into the pond in autumn. Last year's mesh net sagged into the water after rain and was difficult to lift, so suggest a more workable leaf-management option if it fits the limits below. There is no bad smell, and I have not seen gasping, unusual behavior, or fish lying over. Do not treat this as an emergency already in progress.

Yesterday morning the water was 61°F. A test strip showed pH 7.5, nitrite 0, and nitrate about 20 ppm. I have no ammonia kit and am unsure how accurate the strip is; alkalinity and hardness have not been tested. The water level sometimes drops an inch or two per week, but I do not know whether this is evaporation, splashing, or a small leak. I have found no wet patch around the liner. I top up with municipal tap water. A neighbor said, “just leave the hose water sitting overnight,” but I do not know whether that is appropriate for our water or fish. Address that uncertainty rather than treating the suggestion as established fact.

The submersible pump and sponge filter were installed two summers ago. The label says 500 gallons per hour, but I do not know the flow after the hose and filter. The pump runs continuously and has not stopped. Every few weeks the sponge looks brown and the flow seems weaker; I rinse it in a bucket of pond water and reinstall it. The return hose is about 12 feet long and sends water over a flat rock. The outlet is on a GFCI. I have not replaced the pump, hose, or filter media. Recommend reasonable equipment checks and cleaning intervals without assuming anything is broken or defaulting to a larger pump.

**Limits and requested plan**
I can spend up to $180 before tax on useful supplies, but would prefer to use what I already own when reasonable. I have a garden hose, two clean buckets, a hand net, a stiff brush, and gloves. I can spend two or three hours on one weekend to get things under control, then about 15 minutes per week on routine care. I cannot supervise a long weekday job. Avoid algaecide, herbicide, or other pond chemicals as a first choice, and avoid harm to fish, plants, or visiting birds. Two cats sometimes watch the fish from the edge; note practical precautions about tools or materials they could reach, but do not assume they drink from the pond.

Please organize the plan as follows:
1. **Immediate priorities:** Explain what to do first, what can wait, and what to watch over the next few weeks. Give a realistic order for one weekend rather than proposing a complete cleanup all at once. Explain how to remove loose leaves and algae without scrubbing everything bare or stirring up all the bottom material. Say how to dispose of debris or dirty water. Discuss whether partial water changes make sense, and, if so, how to approach them cautiously while the pond volume is uncertain.
2. **Testing and reassessment:** Identify the most important next measurements or tests, how often to check them initially, and which readings or fish signs should prompt a change in the plan. Where advice depends on pond volume, water chemistry, or pump flow, specify what I should measure before acting.
3. **Ongoing care:** Give a simple routine for the rest of spring and summer, then explain what to adjust as leaves begin falling in autumn. My location and winter temperatures are not provided, so ask for local climate information before giving specific cold-weather recommendations rather than assuming a freeze date.

Keep the advice practical for this small pond and within the stated time and budget. I want a usable plan, not a diagnosis of a particular disease or a promise that the water will clear by a certain day. Mention when it would be worthwhile to contact a pond professional or veterinarian, without presenting the fish’s currently normal behavior as an emergency."}, {"id": "arka-v3-train-prompt-0216", "row_sha256": "ceb243ed152318d9527002919479a191efa4b4df1095436bb3b08c59b4f48aec", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need some useful questions for the discussion after a 90-minute contemporary dance workshop at a community arts studio. there were 18 adult participants, with a mix of beginners and people who dance regularly. the instructor used floorwork and partner mirroring, and we have about 20 minutes for the conversation. the point is to hear what the session was like for people and get practical feedback for planning another workshop, not to rate the instructor or put anyone on the spot. could you make around eight to ten open questions, maybe grouped in a sensible way so the facilitator can choose what fits the time? include questions about the pace and instructions, how the floorwork and mirroring felt, and whether people had enough options to take part comfortably. also ask about what participants learned or would like to explore next. keep the wording plain and welcoming for people with different levels of dance experience. don't assume everyone enjoyed the same exercises, and avoid questions that suggest a particular answer. we need questions that can start a real conversation, not a survey with yes-or-no answers.", "output": "Create a set of around eight to ten open-ended questions for a 20-minute discussion following a 90-minute contemporary dance workshop at a community arts studio. The workshop had 18 adult participants, including beginners and people who dance regularly. It included floorwork and partner mirroring.

The questions should help participants describe their experience and offer practical feedback for planning another workshop. Include questions about the pace and instructions, how the floorwork and mirroring felt, whether participants had enough options to take part comfortably, what they learned, and what they would like to explore next. Group the questions sensibly so the facilitator can choose which ones fit the time.

Use plain, welcoming language for people with different levels of dance experience. Avoid putting anyone on the spot, rating the instructor, assuming everyone enjoyed the same exercises, or suggesting a preferred answer. The questions should invite conversation rather than yes-or-no responses."}]
